findings.title: Match statistics written from inside a validation get rolled back / double-counted
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a DB write (increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`) and it is invoked from `validate_each`, i.e. from the record's validation chain. Two consequences: (1) ActiveRecord runs validations inside the save transaction, so when the user save ultimately fails (which is exactly what happens when the email is blocked) the counter update is rolled back and the match is never recorded for any code path that calls `user.save` directly (e.g. `User.create_for_email`, invite redemption); (2) `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` (for the Discourse Hub check) and then `user.save`, so the validator runs twice and a single signup attempt can increment `match_count` twice. Statistics should be updated outside validation (e.g. in the controller/creation flow) or with an atomic `update_column`/`increment!` executed outside the transaction.

findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is exact and case-sensitive, trivially bypassed
findings.body: `should_block?` does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with no normalization, and neither the model nor the migration downcases/strips the stored value. Since user-supplied emails are not normalized before reaching the validator, blocking `spammer@example.com` does not block `Spammer@Example.com` (Postgres string comparison is case-sensitive), so the block is defeated by changing capitalization. Normalize on write (`before_validation { self.email = Email.downcase(email).strip }`) and on lookup, and make the unique index operate on the normalized value.

findings.title: Non-atomic read-modify-write of match_count loses updates
findings.body: `record.match_count += 1; record.save` reads the current value in Ruby and writes it back. Concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email (the common case for a spam wave) will read the same value and overwrite each other, under-counting matches. Use an atomic SQL increment (e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...')`) instead. Also note `record.save` here silently ignores failures (its return value is discarded), so a validation/DB error leaves the counter silently unupdated.

findings.title: rejectedEmails array is defined on the prototype and shared/never reset
findings.body: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is a mutable array literal on the class definition, so it is shared by every instance of `CreateAccountController` and is never cleared. Because `pushObject` mutates this shared array, emails rejected during one modal session stay rejected for the lifetime of the page (and are visible to any other instance), e.g. after an admin unblocks an address or after the user fixes an unrelated server-side error, the email field keeps showing "invalid". Initialize it per instance (in `init`/`setupController`) and reset it when the modal is opened.

findings.title: Blocked-email check is skipped when another email error exists
findings.body: The `record.errors[attribute].blank?` guard means that if the whitelist/blacklist rule already added an error (or any earlier validator added an email error, e.g. uniqueness), `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is never called and the match is neither detected nor counted. The blocked-email statistics therefore silently miss attempts that also trip another email rule, which undermines the `match_count`/`last_match_at` data this feature is built on.

findings.title: Extracted whitelist/blacklist logic is untested in the new validator spec
findings.body: The whitelist/blacklist email-domain logic was moved out of `User#email_validator` into `EmailValidator`, but the new spec only exercises the blocked-email branch with `should_block?` stubbed. There is no coverage for `email_domains_whitelist`/`email_domains_blacklist` behaviour in its new location, nor an integration test proving that `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` on `User` actually rejects a blocked email on save. A regression in the moved code would go unnoticed.
